study.title: Proverbs 9 The invitation of wisdom and the trap of folly
study.overview: Proverbs 9 presents two competing tables: that of Wisdom and the Unwiseness. The first offers life, growth and prudent path; the second seduces with hidden pleasure, but ends in death. The chapter calls the reader to decide between hearing the voice of wisdom or giving in to deception, showing that the choice is not neutral: it shapes the spiritual and moral destiny of the person.

outline.title: The table prepared by Wisdom
outline.explanation: Wisdom is portrayed as a lady of greatness and generosity, with firm house, prepared banquet and public invitation. She especially calls the inexperienced to leave the folly, receive food and walk in the way of prudence. The invitation points to a relationship committed to wisdom, which leads to life.

outline.title: How the person responds to correction
outline.explanation: The text contrasts the reaction of the scoffer and the wise to reproof. Correcting the arrogant usually brings shame to the counselor, while the sage loves who instructs him. The fear of the Lord is presented as the beginning of wisdom, and the responsibility for the answer lies upon each one: wisdom benefits the wise himself; the mockery harms only the mockery himself.

outline.title: The deceptive table of Insensateness
outline.explanation: The foolishness appears as a noisy and ignorant woman, sitting in a visible place and calling the same kinds of people. His invitation promises secret and attractive pleasure, but hides that his guests already walk toward death and the depths of Xeol.

study.context: The notes highlight the image of the banquet in the ancient Near East as an important occasion for celebration, and use this image to show that Wisdom offers a life of communion and commitment. The whole chapter functions as a literary contrast between two public invitations and two final consequences.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that wisdom is not mere accumulation of information, but a life orientation that begins with the fear of the Lord. Wisdom calls the simple because they can still be formed; the mocker resists correction and reaps moral isolation. The chapter also affirms personal responsibility: no one is forced by wisdom or folly; each one responds to the invitation he accepts. Finally, the text shows that sin often dresses in pleasure and secret, but its end is destruction. In evangelical reading, many interpreters see in Wisdom a figure that broadly points to God's redemptive action in calling people to life; this is an interpretation, not a direct statement of the verse.

scholarViews.insight: The number seven communicates greatness and fullness, so that the seven pillars represent the magnificence of the house of Wisdom.
Christ and sin dispute the human heart; the chapter presents both inviting the soul and showing that the result of each choice will be distinct.
The fear of the Lord and the answer to wisdom are presented as a real benefit to the person himself; rejecting wisdom brings personal suffering.

questions: What kind of voice has received more attention in your daily life: that of Wisdom or that of Disaster?
How do you react when someone corrects your life: with defense, contempt or gratitude?
What promises of sin today seem more attractive, but hide destructive consequences?
study.practice: This week, choose a concrete area in which you have been easily seduced by shortcuts, hidden pleasure or defensive pride. Pray asking for fear of the Lord, ask a mature person to speak frankly about this area and practice listening without justifying himself. Also set aside time to read Proverbs 9 aloud, identifying which expressions describe their current posture in the face of correction and advice.
study.uncertainty: The readings of Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke include Christological applications and interpretive expansions that go beyond the literal statement of the text; they were treated here as interpretations. The biblical text provided already brings the identification of Unwiseness as a woman, but does not allow to define with historical or geographical certainty who she would be; therefore, I have kept the literary and theological description without speculation.
